title: Obedience (I.9)
hookLine: being in charge looks like freedom; chapter nine says it's safer to be under direction, and safer to hear advice than give it
tomorrow: if you fixed just one fault a year, where would you start?

lines: SAFER TO HEAR THAN TO GIVE.
cards: Being the one in charge looks like freedom. You pick the plan. Nobody tells you no.
Chapter nine of The Imitation of Christ looks at that picture and turns it around. It's much safer, it says, to stand under obedience than to be in charge. And safer to hear advice than to give it.

teach.b: The chapter was written for a religious community, where obedience to a superior is a promise. It's honest about how that goes: some obey out of necessity, not love, and grumble. But its reason reaches anyone.
Everyone likes their own opinion, it says, and leans toward people who agree.
Who is so wise as to know everything? So don't trust your own view too much; be willing to hear others. Even when your view is good, letting it go for peace, for God's sake, is wiser than digging in.
That's why direction is safer: the person under it has another pair of eyes. Here's a neighbor who says something close.

In the Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, one verse says, put simply: if you find a wise person who points out your faults, as someone would point out hidden treasure, follow that person; it will go better for you, not worse.

teach.h: FOR GOD'S SAKE, OR ON THE PATH.
teach.b: That's the thing to tell a friend tonight: two old traditions both call correction from someone wiser a treasure, not a loss.
And the honest difference. For the Imitation, obedience is for the love of God, in a community where God is among them.
The Dhammapada isn't speaking of obeying God; it points to a wise guide on the path the Buddha taught.

how: Catholic religious make a vow of obedience to their superiors, and lay Catholics may seek a spiritual director or a trusted confessor whose counsel they weigh and follow.

o: a soldier's oath to follow orders in war
doing whatever the loudest person demands
living under direction and hearing counsel

games.q: chapter nine and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: safer under obedience than in charge
faults pointed out, like hidden treasure
for God's sake, or on the Buddha's path

s: obedience in the Imitation means doing whatever anyone tells you
it's living under a superior and hearing counsel, for the love of God.
the chapter says it's safer to hear advice than to give it
who is so wise as to know everything?
the Imitation and the Dhammapada mean exactly the same thing by obedience
both prize correction; the Imitation obeys for God's sake, the Dhammapada follows a wise guide on the Buddha's path.

games.q: a Buddhist classmate says her grandfather corrects how she prunes his bonsai, and she's learned to thank him for it. what's an honest thing to say back?
o: both our traditions call correction a treasure; mine frames it as obedience for God's sake.
our two religions teach exactly the same thing about obedience.
that's only about bonsai, so there's nothing to compare.
games.why: the Dhammapada says follow the wise one who points out your faults like treasure; the Imitation says hearing counsel is safer. shared ground, and a real difference.

practice: Count on your fingers three pieces of advice you once resisted that turned out right, and give each person a moment of thanks. Then let one more come to mind, advice you're resisting now, and hold it as if it might be treasure.

wordCard.voice: Obedience. In chapter nine, living under direction and hearing counsel, safer than ruling by your own opinion.

orig.s: multo tutius est stare in subiectione quam in praelatura
orig.say: MOOL-toh TOO-tsee-oos est STAH-reh in soob-yek-tsee-OH-neh kwahm in pray-lah-TOO-rah
orig.note: Latin, Imitation I.9: it is much safer to stand in subjection than in authority.

carryVoice: Your line: under direction. Another pair of eyes is a gift, even when it stings a little. Good night.

sources.work: The Imitation of Christ (attributed to Thomas à Kempis)
